segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Finally, my brothers and sisters, rejoice in the Lord. To write the same things to you is no trouble for me, and for you it is a safeguard.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Watch out for the dogs, watch out for the evil workers, watch out for the mutilation.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For we are the circumcision, we who worship by the Spirit of God and boast in Christ Jesus and put no confidence in the flesh,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: though I myself have grounds for confidence in the flesh as well. If anyone else thinks they can put confidence in the flesh, I can do so more:

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: circumcised on the eighth day, from the people of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew born of Hebrews; as to the law, a Pharisee;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: as to zeal, a persecutor of the assembly; as to the righteousness that is in the law, found blameless.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But whatever were gains to me, these I have come to count as loss because of Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: More than that, I count everything as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord, for whose sake I have suffered the loss of everything, and I count it dung, so that I may gain Christ

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and be found in him, not having a righteousness of my own that comes from the law, but the one that comes through faith in Christ, the righteousness from God that rests on faith,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that I may know him and the power of his resurrection and a sharing in his sufferings, being conformed to his death,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: if somehow I may arrive at the resurrection from the dead.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Not that I have already obtained this or have already been made perfect, but I press on, if only I may take hold of it, because I was myself taken hold of by Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Brothers and sisters, I do not consider myself to have taken hold of it. But one thing I do: forgetting what is behind and stretching out toward what is ahead,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I press on toward the goal, for the prize of the upward call of God in Christ Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So let all of us who are mature be of this mind; and if on any point you are of a different mind, this too God will reveal to you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Only, whatever point we have reached, let us keep in step with that.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Join together in imitating me, brothers and sisters, and keep your eyes on those who walk in this way, according to the pattern you have in us.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For many are walking—I often told you about them, and now I say it even in tears—as enemies of the cross of Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Their end is destruction, their god is the belly, and their glory is in their shame; their minds are on earthly things.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For our commonwealth is in the heavens, and from it we eagerly await a savior, the Lord Jesus Christ,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: who will transform the body of our lowliness to be conformed to the body of his glory, in keeping with the working by which he is able even to subject all things to himself.

notes.note: The Greek plural is grammatically masculine but was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of men and women. Paul is writing to the whole community at Philippi, which included women he names in the next chapter. Older translations have “brethren” or “brothers”; many recent ones render as here.

notes.traditional: the concision; the mutilation; those who mutilate the flesh
notes.note: Paul plays on two similar words: katatomē (“cutting up, mutilation”) here and peritomē (“circumcision”) in the next verse. He refuses the honored name to those who insist that non-Jewish believers be circumcised, and uses instead a word whose verb in the Greek Old Testament describes forbidden pagan gashing of the body. “Dogs” was a common term of contempt, here turned on these teachers.

notes.phrase: worship by the Spirit of God
notes.note: The earliest and most widespread manuscripts read “of God” (worship by the Spirit of God). Others read “God” as the object, giving “worship God in spirit,” which lies behind the King James rendering. Most modern editions and translations follow the reading translated here.

The Greek word was the ordinary term for a citizens’ gathering and the Greek Old Testament’s term for Israel assembled before God. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and is not wrong, but it now suggests a building or institution. This translation uses “assembly” everywhere so that the reader can see it is one word.

Greek has a single word-family where English has two: righteous and just, righteousness and justice, and the verb “justify.” The word covers being in the right, doing what is right, and God’s action to set things right. Some scholars prefer “justice” or “covenant faithfulness”; the traditional word is kept here and in verse nine.

The word was used both for excrement and for refuse such as table scraps or sweepings, and it carried a note of disgust. Most modern versions choose “rubbish” or “garbage”; the King James has “dung.” Either is lexically sound; the stronger word is used here because the term was not a polite one.

The Greek is literally “faith of Christ,” and the grammar allows two readings: the believer’s faith in Christ, or Christ’s own faithfulness. “Faith in Christ” is the traditional and still majority reading and is followed here. “The faithfulness of Christ” has substantial scholarly support and would make the phrase refer to Christ’s obedient death, with the believer’s faith mentioned at the end of the verse.

The Greek connective can mean “because” or “that for which.” On the second reading Paul presses on to take hold of the very thing for which Christ took hold of him. Translations and commentators are divided. The same verb, “take hold of,” is used for Paul’s striving and for Christ’s seizing of him.

notes.traditional: the high calling; the upward call; called me heavenward
notes.note: The phrase is literally “the above call.” It may mean a call that comes from above, a call that summons upward to heaven, or, continuing the athletic image, the summons of the victor to receive the prize. The rendering leaves these open.

This adjective belongs to the same word-family as “made perfect” in verse twelve, and Greek readers would have heard the echo. It commonly meant full-grown or adult, and that is the likely sense here. Some think Paul is using the word with irony, borrowing a claim to be “perfect” made by others.

In the period the word regularly meant a state or civic body, including a colony of people living abroad under their home city’s constitution, rather than the abstract status of citizenship. Philippi was a Roman colony whose citizens belonged to Rome though they lived far from it, and “savior” and “lord” were titles given to the emperor. Most versions have “citizenship,” which conveys the point well enough; “commonwealth” is closer to attested usage and fits “from it” that follows.

The Greek is plural, a turn of phrase carried over from Hebrew and Aramaic. Most translations flatten it to “heaven”; this translation keeps the plural where the Greek has it and God’s dwelling is meant.

candidates.reason: The plural address to mixed communities recurs throughout the letters and Acts, and versions split between “brothers” and “brothers and sisters”; it needs one policy.
Paul’s uses range from the physical body to human status and to the sinful nature, and translations vary widely (“flesh,” “human effort,” “sinful nature”); a reader needs to see one word.

candidates.rendering: be of … mind / minds are on
candidates.reason: A key verb in Philippians and Romans (also Phil 2:2, 2:5; Rom 8:5; Col 3:2) rendered variously as “think,” “set the mind on,” “have this attitude”; consistency would show the thread.
The figurative sense of conduct recurs across Paul and John, and translations divide between keeping the Semitic “walk” and paraphrasing as “live” or “behave.”
It wavers between “perfect,” “mature” and “complete” across Matthew, Paul, Hebrews and James, and should be coordinated with the register entry for τελειόω.
